title: AI makes starting a company easier than getting a job, but solo founders have no safety net
dek: Durable hit a million users in three months, but the founder says he took a detour: website generation isn't the endgame—handing the entire back office of the service industry to AI is. Being a solo founder isn't more freedom; it's putting every decision on yourself.
why: The first half is founder background and fundraising stories, with average information density; the second half on product judgment, the death of UI, and the pros and cons of solo founding is worth listening to.
who: Founders considering solo founding or already solo founding, and product leads building AI products who are debating whether to keep building UI.
skip: The industry chit-chat and Shopify analogy from 0:00-9:00 can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: 3.5 million sign-ups, half are brand-new businesses
points.body: About 3.5 million people have signed up on Durable to start a business, and more than half are net new—not existing businesses coming online, but people starting a company for the first time. These people aren't in the brainstorming phase; they already have an idea, maybe a bit of revenue, and the first thing they do on Durable is build an online presence, do SEO and GEO, get found on ChatGPT and Google, start advertising and follow up with customers. Clift says this showed him a huge number of businesses he "couldn't have dreamed existed," like decorating porches for Halloween, which can do hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.

points.h: AI website generators are a detour, not the endgame
points.body: Durable's original vision was "Shopify for the service industry," close to a franchise model: franchisees pay $100,000, Durable takes $10,000, and provides the same leads, website, and marketing system. After GPT-2.5 came out, they did a one-week internal hack week, built an AI website generator, and after launching in 2022 it went viral, growing from zero to about a million users in three months and bringing in significant revenue. But they spent a year and a half on that product, and Clift now calls it an "interesting distraction"—a good business, but not the market they wanted to be in. Four years later, they're back to the original vision: an AI-powered "business in a box" for service business owners.

points.h: Users don't want buttons, they want results
points.body: Clift deliberately avoids UI details in customer feedback: everyone says they want to change this button, add this component, customize that, but what they really want is a better-looking, better-performing website. Similarly, appointment scheduling can fall into a rabbit hole of time zones and multiple calendars, but what people really want is "jobs booked." His conclusion: building UI now has extremely low value, first because AI makes UI easy to build, and second because nobody wants to click through a bunch of things—if users never log into Durable and just get one text a day, that's a better experience. The product should be input-output: describe the problem you want solved, and it gets solved.

points.h: You should now actively pick harder problems
points.body: Clift says that since models will keep getting stronger and will make your product obsolete ("maybe it's already obsolete, and at least once more within six months"), you should actively choose harder problems. Durable has millions of people starting new businesses, and making them successful is an extremely hard problem, but once solved, it corresponds to trillions of dollars in GMV and economic value. He also mentions team size: still only six engineers, but "six engineers are roughly equivalent to sixty agents," so adding features is no longer scary, and the real risk becomes "are you building the right thing for the right customers."

points.h: Solo founding is about shedding responsibility to others
points.body: Clift says he didn't deliberately choose to be a solo founder, but his first two co-founder partnerships got stuck on the same thing: misaligned runway and risk. He couldn't help calculating the opportunity cost for the other person—"how much they could make at Amazon, how much in consulting"—and by rational calculation, you should never start a software company. More critically, the psychological burden: with even one co-founder, he felt he had to keep them happy, take care of them, essentially carrying their family's livelihood on his shoulders. Solo founding removed that pressure: "now it's all on me," and he can focus only on the business, be freer to do creative work, and if he fails, only he is affected.

points.h: Built in Vancouver, funded in San Francisco
points.body: Clift's judgment: to win a venture-backed mega-outcome, you probably still have to be in San Francisco; but Vancouver is a great place to build, and San Francisco is a great place to raise money and get inspired. Every time he goes to San Francisco, he thinks "we should work harder, faster, be more ambitious," but that energy often gets in the way of actually building product and understanding customers, creating that lost founder who's "caffeinated, tried a million things, gripping the handlebars but not knowing what they're doing." His approach: company DNA, ambition, and fundraising are Silicon Valley-style, but customers aren't in Silicon Valley—they're in middle America, internationally, and they're solo owners.

In college, Clift cleaned windows and gutters, selling door-to-door. He learned two things: first, desensitization to rejection—nobody will yell at you for knocking and offering help, and they'll forget you in two days or even two minutes; second, volume. Knock on enough doors and you'll close, then a neighborhood "flips": one does it, puts up a sign, and neighbors all follow. He directly compares this to fundraising and cold emails: the worst outcome is they don't read it, and that's probably what will happen. He also says that if building becomes easier because of AI, then sales becomes more valuable.

points.h: Earning your first dollar is a worldview unlock
points.body: Clift thinks one of the most interesting parts of human experience is "earning money yourself," not even in a financial sense. The world is designed around employment, and profits flow to business owners; but earning a dollar yourself is still outside the norm for most people—"I had an idea, and someone paid for it." He says it's like opening a small door, and you become more ambitious, going from twenty or thirty dollars to tens of millions in revenue. He also admits you might try it and find you don't like it, but everyone should try it once, and most people are better at it than they think.
